item.title: Cash takes centre stage as investors rethink AI spending boom
item.description: Investors are increasingly focused on technology companies' cash generation capabilities to fund artificial intelligence investments. Microsoft and Oracle are gaining positive attention from investors, while Alphabet faces challenges due to rising AI costs. Alphabet's spending has surpassed its operating cash flow, raising concerns about its financial sustainability. In contrast, Microsoft's strong cash flow and forecasted growth indicate effective AI investment returns.
item.dc:creator: ETMarkets.com
item.content:encoded: Investors are drawing a sharper line between technology companies that can fund their artificial intelligence ambitions through cash generation and those whose spending is outpacing their operating income. Microsoft and Oracle have won favour on Wall Street, while Alphabet faces pressure as rising AI costs collide with slower growth in its core search business, Reuters reported.Alphabet shares fell over 13% on Thursday while Oracle slipped 4% and Microsoft was down 0.45% at 3:48 pm ET.The divergence signals a shift in investor priorities, with spending alone no longer enough to justify lofty AI expectations.For live updates on US Markets, click here Alphabet’s AI spending outpaces cash generationAlphabet spent 121.4% of its operating cash flow on capital expenditure in the September quarter, compared with 68% for Microsoft, excluding finance leases, according to Reuters. Spending above 100% means a company must rely on cash reserves or borrowing to cover the shortfall.Google’s search revenue grew 12%, missing market expectations of 14.7%, even as CEO Sundar Pichai said search queries were growing at their fastest pace in five years. The slowdown has raised concerns that AI chatbots and agents could challenge the business funding Alphabet’s expansion.Also Read: Alphabet’s AI risks deepen as filing reveals $98 billion in commitments beyond the $1 trillion spendingAlphabet’s capital expenditure could reach $205 billion this year, while Google Cloud revenue more than doubled to $30.71 billion. However, its cash burn reached $9.07 billion, underscoring the strain of its investment programme, Reuters reported.“Microsoft's quarter demonstrated very disciplined growth, whereas Google is burning cash and its core business came in below expectations,” said Melissa Otto, head of research at S&P Global Visible Alpha.Microsoft demonstrates returns from AI investmentMicrosoft generated $18.6 billion in free cash flow in its fiscal first quarter, nearly $10 billion above Wall Street expectations, despite spending $45.2 billion on computing infrastructure. Azure revenue surged 48%, while the company forecast stronger cloud growth for the current quarter, Reuters reported.Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said businesses were moving beyond experimentation with AI towards longer-term commitments.“The shiny object stuff is waning,” Nadella said during an analyst call.Oracle’s plans to curb external financing further reinforced the market’s focus on cash generation, suggesting investors increasingly want evidence that AI investments can support themselves rather than depend on continued borrowing. (Disclaimer: This article is based on inputs from agencies. These do not represent the views of The Economic Times)

item.title: Alphabet’s AI risks deepen as filing reveals $98 billion in commitments beyond the $1 trillion spending
item.description: In a recent regulatory disclosure, Alphabet reveals financial risks linked to its massive AI investments that surpass $1 trillion. The firm might be burdened with nearly $98.5 billion in contingent commitments, including data center leases and chip system repurchases. There are growing apprehensions about the sustainability of Google Cloud's expansion due to a substantial backlog from its collaboration with Blackstone.
item.dc:creator: ETMarkets.com
item.content:encoded: Google parent Alphabet's financial risks related to its artificial intelligence expansion extend beyond the $1 trillion plus in spending commitments it disclosed earlier, and sits at around $98.5 billion as of the September quarter as per its latest regulatory filing, according to a Bloomberg report.The filing on Thursday shows Alphabet could face another $98.5 billion in contingent commitments under certain conditions, up about $23 billion from the previous quarter. These include guarantees for data centre leases, financial backing for partners buying power equipment and potential obligations to repurchase AI chip systems from customers.The disclosures come as investors scrutinise whether surging AI expenditure will generate adequate returns.Also Read: Nasdaq slides over 1% as Alphabet's AI spending revives investor concernsCloud backlog raises questions over growth qualityGoogle Cloud’s backlog climbed to $560.8 billion at the end of September from $513.9 billion three months earlier. However, $16.8 billion of the backlog is linked to Crux AI, a joint venture Alphabet established with Blackstone, according to the filing cited by Bloomberg.Alphabet owns a minority stake in the venture and has pledged up to $10 billion in data centre and energy backstops to support it.For live updates on US Markets, click here The arrangement raises questions about how much of the cloud division’s growth comes from independent customers rather than businesses backed by Alphabet itself.“It does kind of take a little bit of the luster off,” said Dan Morgan, senior portfolio manager at Synovus Trust, as quoted by Bloomberg. “It would be nice if it was coming from a bunch of outside customers. That is something that you do have to raise an eyebrow about — is this a self fulfilling prophecy?”Search monetisation and AI commitments add pressureThe filing also highlights challenges in Alphabet’s core advertising business, which helps finance its AI expansion. Paid clicks on Google Search grew 8% in the third quarter, slowing from 13% in the previous quarter, despite Chief Executive Officer Sundar Pichai saying query growth was the fastest in five years.Chief Business Officer Philipp Schindler said AI Mode queries affected revenue because of “the lower monetization” of those queries. Alphabet is expanding advertising in AI Mode, including into international markets.Other disclosures underline the scale of its AI related exposure. Alphabet may have to repurchase up to $6.6 billion in AI chip systems from customers, while energy guarantees more than doubled to $16.2 billion, Bloomberg reported.The company also acknowledged that autonomous agents had sometimes taken actions “outside of their intended scope” during model testing, as it prepares to expand agent capabilities in Gemini.Together, the disclosures give investors a broader picture of the financial and operational risks accompanying Alphabet’s AI ambitions. (Disclaimer: This article is based on inputs from agencies. These do not represent the views of The Economic Times)

item.title: ECB keeps rates unchanged but points to mounting inflation risk
item.description: The European Central Bank has decided to maintain its current interest rates, signaling concerns over inflation driven by escalating energy costs. Meanwhile, borrowing expenses in France have seen a sharp rise, creating anxiety about the nation’s economic outlook amid political upheaval. ECB President Christine Lagarde's early resignation raises questions about the potential investigation into growing French debt.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: The European Central Bank left interest rates unchanged in a well-telegraphed move on Thursday but warned that inflation risks were on the rise from surging energy costs, which may solidify market bets for a December rate hike.The ECB has raised rates twice this year to prevent an Iran war-induced energy price jump from getting entrenched and has signalled that more may be needed, even if it was not in a hurry without evidence of dangerous second-round inflation effects.In a decision published only hours after ECB President Christine Lagarde announced she would step down early, the ECB warned risks to inflation were skewed to the upside given a recent surge in oil and gas prices. Energy prices have continued to rise, posing upside risks to the inflation outlook and downside risks to the growth outlook, the ECB said in a statement.It added that underlying inflation had remained broadly stable and wages had not shown a material response to higher prices although the increased magnitude and duration of the energy shock were likely to drive up inflation and undermine growth.Deteriorating financing conditions, particularly in France, may complicate the bank's next decision.Borrowing costs have increased sharply in recent months and the flow of credit is expected to slow, putting a brake on economic growth.This achieves the sort of policy tightening an ECB hike would accomplish but also risks financial turbulence as France now has to pay a decades-high 155 basis point premium over Germany to borrow for 10 years. Financing conditions have tightened since the Governing Council's last meeting, which is likely to weigh on inflation and growth, the ECB said.This suggests the ECB will need to walk a narrow path in the months ahead.It must prevent high inflation from becoming embedded as price growth is already twice its 2% target. But it wants to avoid setting off turbulence in markets that could induce a recession or broader financial instability.This is why the vast majority of economists polled by Reuters see just one or two more hikes before the ECB ends the current tightening cycle.Attention now turns to ECB President Christine Lagarde's 1345 GMT news conference, during which she is likely to face questions on what the ECB would do should French borrowing costs surge further.Lagarde is also likely to be asked about her own future after saying she would leave office on February 7, months before her tenure was due to end.Reuters reported this month that the World Economic Forum could appoint Lagarde as its next chair as soon as November, hastening a wider reshuffle at the top of the ECB.FRENCH TURMOIL IN FOCUSThe most immediate challenge for ECB policymakers could be turmoil in bond markets.A global rise in yields, fuelled by stronger growth expectations, higher debt issuance and massive investment linked to artificial intelligence, is pushing up borrowing costs for governments, households and businesses alike.In France, investors have become increasingly uneasy about the country's growing debt burden and uncertain fiscal outlook following this year's elections. Concerns have been amplified by suggestions from parts of the political left that debt held by the ECB could be written off.The result has been a sharp increase in French borrowing costs, with France now paying some of the highest yields in a quarter-century to raise money on bond markets.That has fuelled speculation that the ECB might be forced to respond, if only verbally for now.The ECB's first line of defence would probably be flexible reinvestment of proceeds from bonds acquired during its vast asset-purchase programmes of the previous decade.Beyond that, it could activate its never-used Transmission Protection Instrument, a scheme designed to counter what policymakers deem unjustified market pressure.
